text: Virtual machines fail along with their hardware, so Azure gives administrators two different ways to protect against that: Availability Sets and Availability Zones. They sound similar, and both show up constantly in exam objectives and real architecture reviews, but they protect against very different sizes of failure, and mixing them up is a real design mistake.

An Availability Set spreads VMs across fault domains and update domains inside a single datacenter. A fault domain is a group sharing one power source and network switch, so a power or switch failure doesn't take out every VM at once. An update domain is a group Azure reboots together during planned host maintenance, so a maintenance cycle doesn't restart every instance simultaneously.

You create the set first, then point VMs at it with --availability-set. Azure automatically places each VM in a different fault domain and update domain. That protects against a rack losing power or a maintenance reboot — but every VM in the set still lives in the same datacenter, so a failure of that entire building takes all of them down together.

An Availability Zone, by contrast, is a separate physical datacenter inside the same region, with its own power, cooling, and network. The --zone flag pins a VM to zone 1, 2, or 3. Spread VMs across zones and a failure at the datacenter level, not just a rack, no longer takes the whole application down.

A VM uses one or the other, never both. Availability Zones protect against a bigger failure for the same basic cost and are the modern default wherever a region supports them. Availability Sets still earn their place in regions without zones, or in older deployments built before zones existed there.

You can now choose the right placement mechanism for a VM's fault tolerance, and explain to someone else exactly why one protects against less than the other.
